picks.rationale:
Gary's Take

Getaway day at Great American Ball Park, 89 degrees with the wind blowing out to left, and the Dodgers are trying to close out this four-game set with a bullpen game after Blake Snell's groin sent him to the showers after one inning last night. Cincinnati hands the ball to Brady Singer looking to split the series.

What carries this pick is the shape of the Dodgers' pitching plan. Justin Wrobleski's 3.78 ERA is an All-Star first half wearing a second-half body. Since July 28 he has given up 13 home runs in 26.2 innings, he missed time with left forearm inflammation, and his three outings since returning ran 36, 73 and 25 pitches. He is a fly-ball lefty with a home run problem walking into a homer park with the wind out, and once he is done the ball goes to a Triple-A recall and then a bullpen that used six relievers to cover seven innings yesterday. On top of that, the posted lineup has no Mookie Betts and no Will Smith on a day game after a night game. The Dodgers have scored 4, 4 and 2 runs in this series and went 0-for-11 with runners in scoring position last night. The team on the field today is a lot weaker than the brand the market is pricing at -172.

The best argument against me is real and I am not dodging it. Singer has been awful: 14 earned runs and 11 walks over nine innings in his last two starts, and lefties have hit him for an .883 OPS with 22 homers this season while the Dodgers stack seven left-handed bats against him. Roberts also has Tanner Scott, Brock Stewart and Evan Phillips, none of whom pitched yesterday, to protect a lead. If Singer walks the yard in the first two innings this is over early. I take the Reds anyway because the price is wrong for the matchup, not because Singer is good. Elly De La Cruz hits left-handers at .346 with a 1.051 OPS and just homered in two of three games, Sal Stewart and Juan Brito went a combined 6-for-7 yesterday, and this crowd just watched the Reds take one from this team. At +144 I am being paid as if the full Dodgers showed up today. They did not.

Gary's Take

Series finale at the Trop, 1:10 first pitch, Drew Rasmussen going for the sweep against Jeffrey Springs, back in the building for the first time since Tampa Bay traded him. The Rays are the right side of the moneyline, but at -260 that ticket pays nothing, and the run line is where this game has actually been living. Both games of this series ended one-run: 2-1 in ten innings, then 4-3. That is not a fluke pattern for Rasmussen games. Tampa Bay has won his last ten starts, and five of those ten were by exactly one run, including 1-0 twice. He is 14-5 with a 2.81 ERA and has held opponents to two runs or fewer in 21 of 28 starts, so I expect him to be good. I just do not expect the margin to run away in a dome with a 0.93 park factor.

The part of Oakland that has kept these games tight is the bullpen, and it is legitimately hot. Over the last 30 days Harris (1.42), Hartlieb (1.08), Blewett (2.16), Medina (2.25) and Alvarado (2.45) all carry ERAs under 2.50, and the pen threw 5.1 scoreless innings Wednesday after Basso left in the third. Hartlieb, Roycroft and Rock have not pitched since Sunday or earlier. Tampa Bay's bridge is the thinner one today. Kelly and Booser have worked both games of this series, and setup man Tyler Wells went on the injured list this week. Springs' 5.93 ERA is the number the market is charging for, but his 4.86 xERA and 4.76 road ERA say that number is fragile. That is context for the price, not a forecast, and it is why -260 and -1.5 at -118 both look like overpays to me.

The argument against me is obvious. Springs has allowed 33 home runs in 135 innings and a .912 OPS to left-handed bats, and he has given up four or more runs in 13 of 27 starts. Tampa Bay sends four lefties and a switch-hitter at him plus Caminero and his 41 homers, in a lineup that has scored 5.3 runs a game over its last ten. If that version of Springs shows up, the Rays win big and this ticket is dead by the fourth inning. I am taking the plus-1.5 anyway because it does not need Springs to pitch well. It needs Oakland's pen to do what it has done for a month and Rasmussen's game to look like Rasmussen's games usually look. That is a near-coin-flip run line where I like my side of the coin, at plus money.

Gary's Take

Getaway day at PNC Park, a 12:35 first pitch, and the Brewers are trying to finish a sweep two days after popping champagne in the visitors' clubhouse. Pittsburgh sends out an opener and a taxed pen, and Milwaukee sends out a lineup card that tells you more than the manager's quotes do.

Two things carry this pick. First, Kyle Harrison has allowed 17 earned runs over his last 7.1 innings, and his season is a boom-or-bust story: nine tidy road outings around three detonations that produced a 6.20 road ERA. Nineteen of his 20 home runs allowed came off right-handed bats, and Pittsburgh is sending seven of nine hitters to the plate from the right side with a 7 mph breeze blowing out to center. Cruz, Lowe, and Flores Jr. all cleared the fence last night. His failure mode is not a slow bleed, it is a crooked number, and Murphy has already said the hook is quick. Second, Milwaukee is running a B lineup. Contreras, Yelich, Bauers, and Pratt are all sitting, Mitchell was scratched yesterday with a neck issue, and Naylor at .148 and Sánchez at .206 are in the order. That is not the group that scored 13 and 20 last week. The price at -142 is paying for the Brewers' brand and the A lineup they are not using.

The best argument against me is the Pirates' pen. Dotel has not gone past six outs in any outing since July 20, Mlodzinski threw 38 pitches yesterday, Ramírez has worked two straight days, and the freshest bulk arm is Curtis, who gave up 6 runs in 3 innings his last time out. Milwaukee has Patrick and Stallings fully rested behind Harrison, so if this turns into a bullpen game on both sides, they have the deeper cover. I take Pittsburgh anyway because the lineup that pen has to get through is diminished, and it stacks five left-side bats against a Pirates staff with three left-handed relievers plus Montgomery, who has not allowed a run in 13.1 innings over the last month, and Weaver both rested. Harrison shut this club out for five innings with 10 strikeouts in August, and Pittsburgh has averaged just 3.1 runs over its last ten. That is the risk. At plus money, with the starter this volatile and the opposing lineup this thin, the risk is worth taking.

Gary's Take

Series finale at Coors Field, Thursday afternoon, Michael King on the hill for a Padres club chasing a Wild Card against Tanner Gordon and a Rockies team playing out the string. Two things carry this pick for me, and both of them are about the innings after the fourth. First, Gordon at this ballpark: I went through his full log, and at home he has given up 14 home runs in 53 innings with a 7.47 ERA, against 4 homers on the road. He has never thrown more than 94 pitches in 30 outings and failed to finish the fifth in each of his last two starts, so the base case is four or five innings and then the handoff. Second, who catches that handoff: a Colorado pen carrying a 7.80 ERA in the tracked sample, which Purple Row reports allowed the most runs of any bullpen in baseball this month, and whose three arms from last night all sit on zero days off after 22, 30 and 15 pitches.

Set that against King, who has allowed 5 earned runs over his last 32.2 innings and has gone 96 to 100 pitches every start in that stretch. He is facing a lineup that runs six left-handed bats at a pitcher holding lefties to a .624 OPS over 398 at-bats. If he gives San Diego six or seven, the soft middle of the Padres pen that Colorado beat up on Monday and Tuesday never sees the game, and Miller, Morejon and Rodriguez are all two full days rested for a day game. That is the shape of a game that gets away from the home side late, and with San Diego scoring 6.1 runs a game over its last ten, the run line at -128 is where the price matches the read better than a moneyline near -200.

The honest case against me is the park itself. Colorado has scored 19 runs in three games this series, this lineup is better at home than its record suggests, and King's 3.03 ERA is running well ahead of a 4.42 xERA, which tells me the market is paying for a number that is shinier than the underlying contact. A couple of Coors mistakes and this is 8-7 again like Monday. I take San Diego anyway because the xERA gap is a note on the price, not on today, and today's matchup asks Colorado to win four or five innings of bullpen baseball against a rested, elite back end while their own worst arms are the ones most likely to pitch. That is a margin bet, and I will pay the smaller price for it.

Thursday night on the North Shore, Pitt opens ACC play with Narduzzi coaching his 144th game, Syracuse makes its first road trip of the year off a loss it controlled everywhere but the scoreboard, and the number asks the home team to win by two scores. I am taking the points.

Start with what the number is really pricing. On a neutral field the ratings put this gap at 8.3 points by SP+ and 10.4 by FPI, and the market opened at 10 before drifting to 10.5 with the juice leaning toward the Syracuse side. That tells me the book is anchored on 10 and reluctant to leave it. A spread that sits at the top of the rating range needs a clean four-quarter path for the favorite, and Pitt's path has a hole in it.

The hole is finishing. Pitt ranks 100th nationally at 3.43 points per scoring opportunity. Last week it went 18 plays for a field goal, converted 5 of 18 third downs and did not score after halftime. Some of that was rain, and Heintschel gets a dry track tonight, but the defense he faces has allowed 1.89 points per opportunity, 15th in the country, ranks 10th in points allowed per play and held Cal to 249 yards. Covering 10.5 requires touchdowns, not a string of Chadha field goals, and the evidence so far says Pitt drives stall inside the 40 more often than they end in the end zone.

Then there is the one true mismatch on the board. Syracuse is 31st in offensive explosiveness. Pitt is 126th in explosiveness allowed. Miami (Ohio) hit a 75-yard touchdown pass on this defense and UCF's only score came on a 19-yard throw after its quarterback shook off several sack attempts. Syracuse does not have to move the ball efficiently, and its 89th-ranked success rate says it probably will not. It needs a handful of chunk plays, and it has Hatcher and Ross-Simmons outside, Bacheyie at tight end and a 55-yard Hill run already on film. Narduzzi said himself that his corners have to play really well to win this game. I believe him.

I know the other side. Angeli threw three interceptions against Cal pressure, and UCF's coach said Pitt was bringing pressure on well over half its snaps. Syracuse leads the FBS with 27 penalties for 257 yards. Pitt has allowed 47 rushing yards all season at 1.1 per carry, so the Orange may be throwing 45 times again. Two turnovers into short fields and this ticket is gone. That is the judgment call, and my read is that both defenses stop drives at a top-25 rate, points come in pieces, and a game shaped like that lands inside two scores more often than outside it. The Cal loss was 436 yards to 249 undone by one safety and two missed kicks. I would rather own the team that dominated the yardage at plus 10.5 than the team that needs a field-goal offense to turn into a touchdown offense on a five-day week.

Gary's Take

Rubber game under a closed roof in Houston, with the Astros tied for the AL West lead and ten to play, and the eliminated Royals showing up Wednesday night like a team that wants to ruin somebody's September. Seth Lugo gets the ball for Kansas City against an Astros opener plan, and the line has Houston at -154.

Two things carry this pick for me. First, the back of the game. Lugo has not finished the sixth inning since Aug 19, so Kansas City is handing four innings to a bullpen that reporting ranks last in the majors by FIP and K-BB%, and its three highest-leverage arms, Kimbrel, Pearson and Cruz, all pitched last night. Pearson has three appearances in the last seven days and Cruz has allowed 12 homers in 54.1 innings. Houston's answer in the same innings is Bryan Abreu, at a 1.88 ERA over his last 30 days, and Josh Hader, at 0.85 with 26 saves and none blown, both reported rested and available for tonight. Second, the matchup at the plate. Lugo is allowing a .304 average and .849 OPS to left-handed hitters over 401 at-bats this season, and Yordan Alvarez, who leads the majors in OPS, bats second at home. Lugo's expected ERA sits right on top of his actual mark, so nobody is paying for a mirage here; he is simply a contact-heavy starter with a lefty problem walking into the wrong lineup and the wrong park.

The honest counter is that Houston's bats are cold, 2.6 runs a game over the last five and 3-7 over ten, and tonight's pitching plan is Miguel Ullola opening for rookie Ethan Pecko, whose walks run high. If that goes sideways early, the bridge is Enyel De Los Santos and Bryan King, who both pitched yesterday and have been hit hard for a month. I took Houston anyway because the plan the log shows is coherent: Ullola has struck out ten and walked one in eight major-league innings, Pecko's last turn was 5.2 innings and one run, and if they get through six with a lead the game goes straight to Abreu and Hader. Kansas City has no version of that path tonight. In a game that projects low-scoring and close, the team with the elite ninth inning and the last at-bat is the one I trust.

Gary's Take

Thursday night on the South Side, and the Tigers roll into Rate Field having won seven of ten while the White Sox limp home after Cleveland shoved them out of first place for the first time since the Fourth of July. Framber Valdez against Erick Fedde in the opener of four, and the board calls it a coin flip.

I am taking Detroit, and the pick lives in innings six through nine. Fedde has not finished the sixth in any of his last five starts, so this game is headed to a Chicago bullpen its own manager admits he has been running at playoff intensity. Grant Taylor has been scored on in four straight outings, Sean Newcomb in five of six and told the Sun-Times he has not been himself, and Hagen Smith threw 110 pitches over four appearances in seven days including 30 last night. Will Venable called sending Smith out for a second inning the most-debated decision he made. What is left is Bryan Hudson, Jordan Hicks, and Noah Schultz with two big-league outings this season. Across the field, Detroit's relievers have a 2.13 ERA in the tracked games, Kenley Jansen sits on two full days off with nine straight scoreless outings, and Holton, Sommers, and Kinley each threw under 25 pitches Wednesday. The other half of the read is the starter my briefing had backwards. Valdez has thrown 13 innings without an earned run over his last two turns, pitches to ground balls at a 1.61 GO/AO, and allows barrels at 5.6 percent against Fedde's 8.2. The market is paying a small premium for Fedde's 3.97 ERA, and his 4.67 xERA says that is the fragile number on the board.

The best argument against me is real. Venable stacked seven right-handed bats against a lefty whose most-used pitch, the sinker, is also his worst, and Miguel Vargas at a .959 OPS against lefties and Randal Grichuk at .989 are exactly the hitters who punish it. Chicago is 43-31 at home and has beaten Detroit six of nine. If Vargas and Grichuk get to Valdez early, this card is cooked. I took the Tigers anyway because six innings of a rested Valdez is a smaller exposure than four innings of a pen that has been bleeding for a week, and because Detroit is scoring 5.8 a game over its last ten while Chicago has lost seven of its last nine. At -104 on a game I read as leaning Detroit, the price is on my side.

Gary's Take

Nola versus McLean under the Citi Field lights, with Philadelphia chasing a Wild Card spot and New York opening its final home stand of the season. The books make the Mets a -130 favorite, and I am taking the other side.

The pick rides on one thing: the price is built on a version of Aaron Nola who has not pitched since early August. The market sees a 4.69 ERA and a 6-10 record. What I see is 7 earned runs across his last five starts, a 2.01 ERA in that window, and eight straight outings of three runs or fewer. His xERA sat at 4.07 all year, so the market has been paying for a fragile ugly number, not a solid one. Meanwhile McLean's shiny 3.24 has cracks in the process: 16 walks in 30 innings over his last five, 25 strikeouts in that span against a season rate near 10 per nine, and 10 hits with two homers at Yankee Stadium last time out. This is closer to a coin flip on the mound than +110 says.

The second lever is the Mets offense. Seven runs in their last four games, Lindor 2-for-16, Soto 3-for-16, and the bottom of the order tonight is Alvarez, Baty and Morabito with Semien out. Lindor and Young both carry sub-.700 OPS marks at night. Philadelphia brings Harper at a 1.009 OPS against right-handers and Schwarber at 1.028 with runners on base. If McLean's walks continue, those two are the swing. New York's bullpen also took a real hit inside the last 24 hours: Stock and Duarte went on the IL yesterday, and Weisenburger and Yan combined for 84 pitches last night. Behind Lavender, Núñez and Senga, it is thin.

The best argument against me is McLean's July start against this exact lineup, 6 shutout innings, 2 hits, 10 strikeouts, plus Soto's 1.017 OPS at home and Nola's 5 homers allowed in 11 innings against the Mets this year. Those are real. But that McLean gem was one game two months ago before the walks crept in, Nola's Mets homers came at Citizens Bank Park and tonight is a 0.95 park, and Soto cannot carry a lineup producing seven runs in four games by himself. The Phillies have the stakes, a 43-34 road record, the 5-4 season series edge, and a starter who has matched the favorite pitch for pitch for six weeks. Plus money on that is the bet.

Gary's Take

Under the closed roof at Globe Life Field, Texas goes for the sweep with a bullpen game, while Boston hands the ball to Sonny Gray trying to stop a two-game slide. This one comes down to who is actually pitching, and that is the whole pick.

The Rangers are not starting Tyler Alexander in any real sense. His log shows he has been a one-inning reliever all year, so he opens and hands it to Cody Bradford, who is 0-5 with a 4.72 ERA in seven starts since returning from elbow surgery. His last two outings were 4 innings and 5 runs with three homers, then 4 innings and 3 runs with a single strikeout. Behind him the pen is stretched thin. Skip Schumaker said after last night, "We didn't have Latz available. We didn't have Garcia available today," and both are on one day of rest with no report clearing them. Nathan Eovaldi threw 46 pitches over 4 innings last night, so the arm that saved Wednesday is gone. The fresh Texas relievers are the ones with the worst recent numbers. On the other side, Gray has thrown 31 innings with 9 earned runs over his last five starts, held this Texas lineup to 1 run with 7 strikeouts in June, and hands off to Garrett Whitlock and Aroldis Chapman, both on three days' rest with ERAs under 2.00. Joc Pederson's scratch today also pulls a 26-homer bat out of the lineup, and that is not in any of the Rangers' recent scoring numbers.

The honest case against Boston is the offense. It has scored 3.2 runs a game over five and just 2 and 3 in this series, and Texas is riding a four-game streak at home where it is 42-32. Gray's ERA also runs well under his expected ERA, so the market is paying for a somewhat fragile number. I take Boston anyway because the runs Boston did not score came against deGrom, Gore and Eovaldi, not against Bradford's current form, and because if this game is close in the seventh, Boston has the rested elite arms and Texas has Junis on zero days and a pen carrying a 4.50 ERA in tracked games. Erik Miller's meltdown last night is a real worry for the bridge, but Chad Tracy has rested options around him. At -126 the market is pricing near a coin flip in a game where Boston holds the better starter, the better bullpen, and the fresher bullpen. I'll pay that.

Gary's Take

Thursday night in Anaheim, the Twins roll in off a 13-inning marathon at Target Field and a flight west across two time zones to open a four-game set against the Angels, with Walbert Ureña taking the ball against Taj Bradley. The market has this as a coin flip at -108 both ways with a 7.5 total, and that is the whole reason I am on the home side. A game priced to be close late gets decided by the arms that pitch the seventh, eighth and ninth, and tonight those arms are not equal.

The Twins used six relievers last night: Hoffman, Minter, Gómez, Funderburk, Adams and Nance, with Adams throwing 34 pitches over three innings. Gómez blew his first save of the season after 22 straight conversions and has given up five earned runs over his last three outings. The two relievers who did not pitch last night, Morris and Rogers, each threw 30 or more pitches the night before, and Morris carries an 11.88 ERA over the last 30 days. Twins relief has a 5.94 ERA in the tracked window against 3.53 for the Angels. On the other side, Suzuki only used Peralta and Farris in last night's blowout loss. Watson, Fermin and Saucedo each had yesterday off, and those three have combined for six earned runs over the last month. Add a Twins lineup that lost Larnach today and Culpepper to the IL yesterday, that has scored 2.7 runs a game over its last ten, and that plays a 6:38 local start after a 13-inning night and a plane ride. That is a spot.

The best argument against me is Bradley. He has allowed 10 earned runs with 39 strikeouts over 29.2 innings in his last five starts, and he faces an Angels offense hitting .234 with a .680 OPS. If he goes seven, the Twins' bullpen problem mostly disappears. I took the Angels anyway because Ureña's contact profile, a 5.6 percent barrel rate against and a 36.4 percent hard-hit rate, lines up well with a thinned-out Twins lineup, and because Bradley has allowed 17 home runs to lefties this year with Meckler, Ballesteros and Lowe sitting in the Angels' top six. Ureña's 2.88 ERA is fragile against a 3.40 xERA, so I am not paying for a shutdown start, just a competitive one. At an even price, I want the side whose best relievers had yesterday off and whose opponent is on the wrong end of the schedule.

Orchard Park opens a $2.1 billion building on a Thursday night, Bruce Smith gets the ceremony, and two of the three highest-scoring offenses in the league over the last 50 games walk in on four days' rest. The number has drifted from a field goal and a hook to nearly a touchdown since Sunday night. I'm taking the points.

The move tells you what the market is paying for. Detroit lost Christian Mahogany and Blake Miller during Sunday's game, both are out tonight, and Larry Borom draws Greg Rousseau after Rousseau posted two sacks and two forced fumbles in Houston. That is real, and it is why this is 5.5 and not 3.5. But it is also the whole Buffalo case, and it is now in the price.

What isn't in the price is how Detroit's one true strength lines up against Buffalo's one true weakness. Jahmyr Gibbs carried 29 times for 156 yards and two scores on Sunday and touched the ball 34 times. Buffalo allowed 136.2 rushing yards per game last season, 28th in the league, gave up 124 to Houston, and was gashed at 5.9 per carry before halftime. Detroit ran 73 plays against New Orleans, converted four of five red-zone trips, and held Jared Goff to a 22 percent pressure rate, second lowest in the league, mostly after Mahogany had already left. That is a ball-control offense against a run defense that has not proven it can get off the field, and it is exactly the profile that keeps a plus-5.5 ticket alive deep into the fourth quarter.

Buffalo's defense is a new scheme and it looked like one. Houston ran 73 plays, held the ball for nearly 13 more minutes, converted 7 of 16 third downs, and rolled up 398 yards. Jim Leonhard called it a lot of ugly, said his players looked around unsure of the answer when things unraveled, and flagged crowd noise in his own building as a communication problem. This unit sat in zone on 81 percent of snaps. Amon-Ra St. Brown finished third in the NFL in yards against zone in each of the last two seasons and just caught 10 balls with two touchdowns.

Then there is how Buffalo actually won. It trailed 31-30 with 3:13 left, took over at its own 4, had James Cook fumble and its own guard recover, saw the go-ahead throw nearly intercepted on the previous snap, and needed a strip-sack with 10 seconds left to survive a defense that led the league in yards allowed last year. Its inside run game succeeded on a third of its snaps and it went 1 of 3 in the red zone. Josh Allen was brilliant, 334 yards and five completions of 30-plus, and he will get his shots against a Detroit secondary that just gave up 410 to a rookie. That is the risk I'm accepting, and it is the reason this is a spread ticket and not a moneyline.

The rest of the game favors the team getting points. Aidan Hutchinson had two sacks and ten pressures against a line that just allowed two sacks, Detroit's front produced five sacks and nine hits, and both teams score at a rate where a 5.5-point margin gets covered by one possession swinging either way. I'll take the offense built to shorten this game and the cushion that comes with it.
